How it works

Simulation and execution

Each trade starts with the stock price normalized to 1 and the rally still active. Rally age advances one trading day at a time. We reuse the same random shocks across scenarios and entry days.

A break applies one downside shock drawn from the range you choose. After that, the stock has an expected daily return of −2%. The survival chart uses the daily break probabilities from rally onset.

We check exits at daily prices. On a move of at least 25% in either direction, an eligible exit may get a price penalty. Margin can lose more than the committed equity when the first observed liquidation price is low. Calls use a Black–Scholes benchmark. Entry implied volatility defaults to each scenario’s annualized stock volatility. You can set a fixed value across scenarios, vary the call fee, and change implied volatility after a break for early exits. Expiring calls settle at intrinsic value.

Research behind the scenarios

Retail buying surges have been followed by reversals on average. A working paper on potential gamma squeezes reports continued gains in a sample selected for persistent hedging pressure. These studies motivate the different scenarios. The lab uses illustrative numbers.

For a real stock, observations such as short interest, float, borrow fees, and announced offerings can help you choose which assumptions to stress-test.

  • Barber et al., Attention-Induced Trading and Returns
  • Zaynutdinova et al., Seeking Gamma
